Differential abundance: CSF proteome in Alzheimer’s disease (PXD016278)

Handling of missing values

Missing values are more frequent in controls than in AD after adjusting for batch and age (see QC report), so their treatment can bias the AD vs. control comparison. Three treatments were compared on the same model (~ group + batch + age + sex): limma on observed values only, limma after left-censored imputation (down-shifted normal, 1.8 SD shift, 0.3 SD width), and proDA, which models the probability of a value being missing as a function of intensity without imputing.

Left-censored imputation inflates effect sizes across the proteome, most strongly for protein groups with more missing values in controls, and changes the set of significant protein groups substantially. Limma on observed values agrees closely with proDA; discordant protein groups lie near the FDR threshold with near-identical fold changes. proDA is used for the main analysis; limma on observed values with sample quality weights is reported as a sensitivity analysis.

Differential abundance

Main model: proDA, ~group + site + age + sex, AD vs control, Benjamini-Hochberg FDR. Site (rather than MS batch) is used because each site was measured in a single batch and site separates Kiel (controls only) from Magdeburg.

Sensitivity analyses

Results are unchanged without the runs flagged for blood contamination and after renormalization (the renormalized list differs only near the FDR threshold, as all fold changes shift by the small diagnosis-associated offset seen in QC). Limma with sample weights recovers the same effects with more power. Adjusting for the plasma-protein score, which is lower in AD, reduces the significant set to a core of protein groups. The score admits three readings that these data cannot separate: a confounder (blood–CSF barrier permeability), a mediator of disease effects, or a compositional effect of normalization. On the last reading, when many brain-derived proteins rise, the relative share of plasma proteins falls; consistent with it, 67% of all protein groups correlate negatively with the score, and the plasma adjustment shrinks the fold change of proteins higher in AD by a median of 42%. Adjusting for the score may then remove part of the disease signal. Both tiers are reported, and the barrier-robust core is read as a conservative lower bound, not as the specific signal.

Of the 67 protein groups lower in AD, 61 lose significance after the plasma adjustment, whereas most of those higher in AD remain. Lower levels in AD are largely explained by the plasma-protein balance, which may itself partly reflect the rise of brain-derived proteins.

Barrier-robust core

The core (50 protein groups; MAPT is excluded because diagnosis is defined from CSF tau) is dominated by glycolytic enzymes (ALDOA, ALDOC, PKM, LDHA, GPI, ENO2, PGK1), 14-3-3 proteins (YWHAZ, YWHAG, YWHAE) and established CSF markers of AD (SOD1, UCHL1, SMOC1, SPP1, FABP3), mostly cytosolic proteins higher in AD. Glycolytic enzymes in CSF most likely indicate release from damaged cells rather than a change in metabolism. The glycolytic signature was also reported in the original study.

Diagnostic classifier

An elastic-net logistic regression (α = 0.5, penalty chosen by inner 5-fold cross-validation, lambda.1se) classifies AD vs control from the proteome. The missing-value filter (≤ 20% missing), protein selection, imputation of missing values (half the training minimum) and scaling are learned within each training split. MAPT is excluded, as diagnosis is defined from CSF tau, and Kiel is excluded, as its controls are age-mismatched and include no AD. Performance is estimated by 10 × 5-fold nested cross-validation and by leave-one-site-out validation, against an age + sex baseline.

A median of 978 protein groups passed the missing-value filter in each training split.

Calibration slope 2.67 and intercept 0.02 (ideal: 1 and 0); a slope below 1 means predictions are too extreme, above 1 too conservative. The proteome outperforms the age + sex baseline (paired DeLong test, p = <1e-04).

The proteome discriminates AD from controls well beyond age and sex. Across sites, performance is maintained for Magdeburg and lower for Berlin and Sweden. Berlin is the largest cohort, so the model is trained on fewer samples when it is held out, and its controls are mostly patients with other neurological diagnoses. Sweden quantifies fewer proteins: many protein groups selected on the other two sites are frequently missing there and are imputed from the training minimum. When the missing-value filter was computed on all samples, test site included, Sweden reached 0.86; the lower value is the honest estimate of transfer to a new site. The most stable predictors (14-3-3 proteins, glycolytic enzymes, SPP1, SMOC1) are the same proteins as the barrier-robust core of the differential abundance analysis; both analyses use the same samples, so this is consistency rather than independent confirmation. The next section quantifies how much of this signal is explained by the CSF biomarkers that define the diagnosis.

Circularity of the diagnostic label

Diagnosis is biochemical: AD requires high CSF tau and low amyloid, with the amyloid measure and thresholds differing by site. Every AD case has t-tau above 400 pg/ml, so any protein that rises with neurodegeneration is associated with the label by construction. t-tau and Aβ42 are the only biomarkers measured at all three sites with AD cases (n = 181; p-tau is missing in Berlin and Aβ42/40 in Sweden). The analysis uses the barrier-robust core without MAPT (50 protein groups), summarised as a signed score: the mean z-score across the core, with proteins lower in AD inverted, so that higher is more AD-like.

The core behaves as a continuous marker of neurodegeneration rather than of diagnosis. The score rises with t-tau within AD and within controls, with similar slopes, and individual core proteins track t-tau within each group (26 of 50 in AD, 27 in controls; FDR < 5%). In Berlin, controls with t-tau in the AD range lie between controls with normal tau and AD, but they also have less tau than AD (median 466 vs 804 pg/ml). Adjusting for t-tau reduces the AD effect on the score by 83%, to a non-significant value, and no core protein retains an AD effect at FDR < 5%. Since the label combines high tau with low amyloid, the tau-adjusted AD effect mainly reflects amyloid status: there is no evidence that the core tracks amyloid beyond tau, although the confidence interval does not exclude a small effect. Adjustment for a covariate measured with error tends to under-adjust, so the share explained by tau is, if anything, underestimated.

Within AD in Berlin, a higher score goes with a lower MMSE, in the expected direction but with a single exploratory test (n = 33). The two biomarkers that define the label reconstruct it almost perfectly (AUC 0.98), above the proteome classifier (0.88): the classifier largely relearns tau-related neurodegeneration and is not evidence of diagnostic value beyond CSF tau and amyloid.
